title: Nomenclature and General Principles of Organic Chemistry
summary: Organic compounds are classified as acyclic (open chain) and cyclic (alicyclic and aromatic: benzene and its derivatives); a functional group is the atom or group that determines the chemical properties (–OH alcohol, –CHO aldehyde, >C=O ketone, –COOH acid, –NH2 amine, –SH thiol, –X halide). A homologous series is a family with the same functional group differing by CH2 (e.g. alkanes CnH2n+2, alkenes CnH2n, alkynes CnH2n−2). IUPAC rules: select the longest continuous chain containing the principal functional group; number it from the end giving the lowest locant to the functional group, then to multiple bonds and substituents; write substituents alphabetically; use the suffix for the principal group (-ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, -thiol, -amine) and the prefix for others (halo, nitro, alkoxy). Priority order: –COOH > –SO3H > –COOR > –COCl > –CONH2 > –CN > –CHO > >C=O > –OH > –SH > –NH2 > C=C > C≡C. Examples: CH3CH2SH ethanethiol; CH3CH(OH)CH3 propan-2-ol; CH3COCH3 propanone; (CH3)2CHCOOH 2-methylpropanoic acid.

Structural isomerism: chain (butane and 2-methylpropane), position (propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol), functional (ethanol and methoxymethane), metamerism (diethyl ether and methyl propyl ether) and tautomerism (keto–enol). Stereoisomerism: geometrical (cis/trans in but-2-ene) and optical (a carbon with four different groups, chiral centre). Inductive effect: permanent polarisation of a σ bond by an electronegative atom or group; –I groups (–NO2, –CN, –COOH, –F, –Cl, –OH, –OR) withdraw electrons and +I groups (alkyl groups) release electrons; order of –I: NO2 > CN > COOH > F > Cl > Br > I. Electromeric effect (temporary, in presence of an attacking reagent), resonance (mesomeric) effect (delocalisation of π electrons/lone pairs, e.g. benzene, carboxylate ion) and hyperconjugation (delocalisation of σ electrons of C–H adjacent to a carbocation, free radical or double bond) explain the stability of species.
## Reaction intermediates and types of reactions

Homolytic fission of a bond gives free radicals (each atom takes one electron); heterolytic fission gives ions – a carbocation (C+, electron deficient, sp² planar) and a carbanion (C−, pyramidal). Stability of carbocations: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH3+ (more alkyl groups give +I and hyperconjugation); free radicals have the same order; stability of carbanions: CH3− > 1° > 2° > 3°. Electrophiles are electron-seeking (H+, NO2+, carbocations, BF3, AlCl3); nucleophiles are electron-rich (OH−, CN−, NH3, H2O, Cl−). Types of reactions: substitution (SN1 and SN2), addition (electrophilic on alkenes, nucleophilic on carbonyls), elimination and rearrangement. Purification of organic compounds: crystallisation, sublimation, distillation (simple, fractional, steam, vacuum), chromatography. Qualitative analysis: Lassaigne's test (N, S and halogens); quantitative: Dumas and Kjeldahl for nitrogen, Carius for halogens.

objective: (a) Which compound forms the ethyl carbocation? (b) Give two examples of nucleophiles.
(a) Bromoethane/chloroethane (C2H5X) by heterolytic fission of the C–X bond: C2H5Br → C2H5+ + Br−. (b) OH−, CN− (also NH3, H2O).

vsa: What is heterolytic fission? What are the species formed?
Cleavage of a covalent bond in which the shared pair goes to one atom, forming a cation and an anion (carbocation or carbanion). They initiate reactions as electrophiles or nucleophiles.
October 2024
What is the –I effect? Give two groups showing it.
The permanent displacement of the electron cloud of a σ bond towards a more electronegative atom or group; –NO2 and –COOH (also –CN, –Cl) show –I effect.
April 2026
Why is a tertiary carbocation more stable than a primary carbocation?
Three alkyl groups release electrons by +I effect and provide more hyperconjugation structures (nine C–H bonds), dispersing the positive charge.
October 2025
Write the IUPAC names of CH3CH2SH and CH3CH2CHO.
Ethanethiol and propanal.
October 2025
What is hyperconjugation? Give one example.
Delocalisation of σ electrons of a C–H bond adjacent to an unsaturated centre or carbocation; the ethyl carbocation CH3CH2+ is stabilised by it.
Distinguish between an electrophile and a nucleophile with one example each.
An electrophile is electron-deficient (accepts a pair), e.g. NO2+; a nucleophile is electron-rich (donates a pair), e.g. OH−.
What are isomers? State the isomerism shown by but-2-ene.
Compounds having the same molecular formula but different structures; but-2-ene shows cis–trans (geometrical) isomerism.
What is a homologous series? Give two characteristics.

A series of compounds with the same functional group, with successive members differing by a CH2 unit; they have a general formula and similar chemical properties with gradation in physical properties.
sa: Write the IUPAC names of (a) CH3CH(CH3)CH2OH (b) CH3CH2CH(Cl)CH3 (c) CH3CH2COOH.
Explain the stability of carbocations with the order of stability and reasons.

3° > 2° > 1° > CH3+. Alkyl groups donate electrons through the +I effect and through hyperconjugation (the number of C–H hyperconjugative structures increases from 0 in CH3+ to 9 in (CH3)3C+), which disperses the positive charge.
Explain the inductive effect and its effect on the acidity of carboxylic acids.

The permanent polarisation of a σ bond by an electronegative group; –I groups such as Cl stabilise the carboxylate and increase the acidity (ClCH2COOH is stronger than CH3COOH), while +I groups (alkyl) decrease it (HCOOH is stronger than CH3COOH).
Distinguish between structural and stereo isomerism with examples of chain and optical isomers.

Structural isomers differ in the connectivity of atoms (butane and isobutane). Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different arrangement in space (cis/trans-but-2-ene, d- and l-lactic acid, which has a chiral carbon).
What are free radicals? How are they formed? Give the order of stability.
Neutral species with an unpaired electron formed by homolytic fission with heat, light or a peroxide (Cl2 → 2Cl•). Stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.
How are organic compounds purified by (a) crystallisation (b) fractional distillation?

(a) The impure solid is dissolved in a hot solvent and filtered; on cooling, pure crystals separate. (b) A mixture of liquids with close boiling points is heated through a fractionating column; the component of lower boiling point distils first.

(a) Select the longest chain containing the principal functional group; number it to give the lowest locant to the principal group, then to multiple bonds and substituents; name substituents alphabetically; use the suffix of the principal group (-ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, -amine, -thiol, -ene).
(b) Butan-2-ol; ethanoic acid; ethanamine; but-2-ene; ethanethiol.
(a) Explain inductive, resonance and hyperconjugation effects with examples. (b) Arrange CH3COOH, ClCH2COOH and FCH2COOH in increasing order of acidic strength and explain.

(a) Inductive: permanent polarisation of σ bonds (–Cl). Resonance: delocalisation of π electrons (carboxylate ion, benzene). Hyperconjugation: C–H σ electrons delocalised into an adjacent empty p orbital (ethyl carbocation).
(b) CH3COOH < ClCH2COOH < FCH2COOH. The –I effect of F is greater than that of Cl, stabilising the anion more.

(a) Distinguish between homolytic and heterolytic fission. (b) What are carbocations, carbanions and free radicals? Give the order of the stability of carbocations. (c) Name two electrophiles and two nucleophiles.

(a) Homolytic: each atom gets one electron, giving radicals; heterolytic: the pair goes to one atom, giving ions.
(b) Carbocation: positive carbon with six electrons (sp², planar); carbanion: negative carbon with a lone pair (sp³, pyramidal); free radical: carbon with an unpaired electron. Stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH3+.
(c) Electrophiles: H+, NO2+; nucleophiles: OH−, CN−.
(a) Explain different types of structural isomerism with one example each. (b) Draw the cis and trans isomers of but-2-ene and write the reason for geometrical isomerism.

(a) Chain – butane and 2-methylpropane; position – propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol; functional – ethanol and methoxymethane; metamerism – diethyl ether and methyl propyl ether; tautomerism – keto and enol forms.
(b) cis-but-2-ene has both CH3 groups on the same side of the C=C; trans has them on opposite sides. Geometrical isomerism arises from restricted rotation about the C=C double bond with two different groups on each carbon.
